results.summary: This design implements a SUBLEQ one-instruction-set computer (OISC) CPU in Verilog. It executes the SUBLEQ instruction, which subtracts one memory value from another and branches if the result is less than or equal to zero. The CPU requires an external RP2040 or similar microcontroller to act as 16-bit memory, communicating via read and write latches with byte-serial data transfer. The project is notable for demonstrating a minimal CPU architecture on a Tiny Tapeout tile, but it cannot function standalone without external memory hardware.

This is a differential RF-DC rectifier designed in Sky130 for passive RFID and RF energy harvesting experiments. It converts an RF input signal into a DC output voltage, with three analog pins for the differential RF input and the rectified output. The design is implemented as an analog block and does not include digital control logic. No testing details or external hardware requirements are provided in the documentation.

This design is a 4-state finite-state machine that controls a water pump based on two binary level sensors, with an error flag for impossible sensor combinations. It is intended for fluid level detection and control, and can be tested by driving the sensor inputs and observing the pump output, error flag, and state outputs. External hardware includes two level sensors, a pump driver circuit (such as a relay or MOSFET), and optional LEDs for status indication. The project is part of the IEEE Open-silicon 2026 initiative and includes cocotb tests covering all state transitions.

This design implements a Physical Coding Sublayer (PCS) with 8b10b encoding and decoding, asynchronous clock domain crossing FIFOs, and a link training state machine for a half-duplex serial link. It operates between a 66 MHz link clock and a 10 MHz system clock, and can be tested using an RP2040 for functional validation or an FPGA for at-speed 66 MHz testing. External hardware for full validation includes a 3.3V FPGA and jumper wires, while basic functional tests can be done with just the demoboard. The design is notable for its compact implementation of a high-speed serial communication protocol on a Tiny Tapeout tile.

This is a multiplayer reaction time game with VGA display output at 640x480 resolution, supporting Classic and Target Match modes for one or two players. It is controlled by push buttons and switches, and displays reaction times and winner information on a VGA monitor. External hardware includes a VGA monitor with a resistor DAC, momentary push buttons, and switches. The design is notable for being a complete game implementation on a Tiny Tapeout tile, using the Tiny VGA pinout.

This design is a pre-trained Binary Neural Network (BNN) for 8x8 MNIST digit classification, implemented in SystemVerilog. It serially loads a 64-bit image and outputs a 4-bit prediction (0-9) after processing, with a reported test accuracy of 70%. The network consists of 18 neurons and is combinational for minimal area, requiring no external hardware for operation. The project is notable for being a silicon-hardened neural network accelerator on a Tiny Tapeout tile, albeit with reduced accuracy due to area constraints.

This design implements a 2x2 systolic-array Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) that performs signed 8-bit matrix multiplication with 16-bit accumulation, optional fused transpose, and ReLU activation. It uses a pipelined streaming architecture that allows overlapping input and output operations, and is controlled via a simple handshake interface. External hardware such as a microcontroller or FPGA is needed to provide input data and read results, but no other external components are required. The project is notable for being a compact matrix multiplication accelerator on a Tiny Tapeout tile.

This design is a test module for learning about scan chains and Design for Testability (DFT) concepts. It contains two 4-bit universal shift registers, one of which can be configured to exhibit stuck-at faults via the ERR input, and both can be placed in scan mode for testing. The module can be used to practice scan chain operation and fault detection, and may require an FPGA or microcontroller to manipulate the inputs. The project is notable for being an educational tool for understanding scan chain testing and fault injection.

This design implements a lightweight AES S-box using composite field arithmetic, performing the non-linear transformation required for 4-bit operations. It takes a 4-bit input and produces a 4-bit output, which can be verified against the standard AES S-box table. No external hardware is required for basic operation, as the S-box is a purely combinational logic block. The project is notable for its compact implementation of a cryptographic primitive on a Tiny Tapeout tile.

This is a mixed-signal design that implements a UART-programmable controller capable of selecting between different analog circuits such as inverters or MOSFET switches. It uses a UART interface for configuration and data transmission, with baud rate selection via input pins, and provides analog outputs on four pins. External hardware includes a voltage supply and an oscilloscope for observing the analog outputs. The project is notable for combining digital UART control with analog circuit selection on a Tiny Tapeout tile.
